problem: The answer says the cosecant-squared pattern 'reduces gain at low elevation'. This is backwards. The pattern keeps high gain near the horizon and reduces gain at high elevation angles (short ranges). As written, the student learns the opposite of how the pattern works.
fix: answer: The gain is shaped as csc²θ, so it is reduced at high elevation angles (short slant ranges) and kept high near the horizon. A target at constant height then gives a more even echo as its range changes.

problem: 'It trades gain at low elevation for a more uniform echo' contradicts the main text, which correctly says gain falls above the horizon. The gain given up is at high elevation angles, not low ones.
fix: A cosecant-squared pattern is not a pencil beam. It gives up gain at high elevation angles (near overhead, short range) so that echoes from targets at constant altitude are more uniform as range changes.

problem: 'A common search radar moves the feed, not the dish, to scan the beam' overgeneralises. Most simple 2D search radars rotate the whole antenna; feed movement is used in some sets, for example nodding-feed height finding on top of a rotating dish.
fix: Some radars scan by moving the feed instead of the heavy dish, for example a nodding feed used for height finding while the dish rotates in azimuth. Many simple search radars just rotate the whole antenna.

problem: Pulse rise time and flat top are said to set 'the smallest usable range'. The minimum range is set mainly by the pulse width τ and the duplexer recovery time; rise time mainly affects the pulse spectrum and spectral splatter.
fix: Rise time and flat top matter because they set the pulse spectrum; the smallest usable range is set mainly by the pulse width and the duplexer recovery time.

problem: CFAR appears in the figure but is never expanded anywhere in the chapter, so a student meeting the acronym for the first time cannot read it.
fix: Write the note as 'I and Q, CFAR (constant false alarm rate)', or add one sentence in Section 3 defining CFAR as a threshold that adapts to the local clutter level.
